ground_truth.title: I Quit Being a Digital Nomad (& here's what you should know about the lifestyle)
ground_truth.author: Andrea Valeria
ground_truth.main_content:
After years of remote work across multiple countries, I realized why most nomads burn out & what to do to actually maximize your freedom & earnings.

The digital nomad life looks like freedom… and in many ways, it is. But after doing it for years, I hit a point where I realized something most people don’t say out loud:

It’s fun. It’s also exhausting. And if you don’t do it the right way, it can mess with your work, your money, and your long-term goals.

So, in this article I wanted to share with you what being a digital nomad actually meant for my life, what I loved about it, what burned me out, and the shift I made when I realized I needed something more sustainable.

Here’s what I’ll be talking about in this post

How my remote work journey started

The perks that make it worth it

My final opinion: Should you do it, or not?

What changed when I became self-employed

What I recommend you do to maximize your stability, freedom & earnings

What is a digital nomad, really?

A lot of people think a digital nomad is simply “someone who moved abroad” or “someone who is traveling.”

But while those 2 can be factors, it is more specific than that: being a digital nomad is working remotely while constantly traveling — moving from place to place and continuing to work the entire time.

Important: You can be a remote worker without being a digital nomad

…which means you work remotely (whether you have a remote job, freelance remotely or manage your business virtually).

You can be a remote worker who mostly works from home or who has a home base and is not on the road 24/7.

But, to be a digital nomad you must be a remote worker— because you need that income coming in. If you’re just traveling all the time and not working, you wouldn’t be considered a digital nomad— you’d just be a full-time traveler.

Both terms should not be used interchangeably. They are NOT the same thing.

OK, now that we got this out of the way, let’s keep talking about being a digital nomad.

It’s not a vacation. You’re not “off.” You’re working while traveling… just in a different location every few weeks (or every month, or every few months). The travel speed is up to each person, but to be a digital nomad, you should be constantly moving. If you’ve settled in another country, you’d just be an ‘expat.’

How my remote work journey started

I landed my first remote job in 2015, and my goal was simple: I wanted to travel and live in many different places.

So I picked a place I had never been to (Buenos Aires, Argentina), and moved there. No reason at all. I just picked any place I wasn’t familiar with to add to the excitement of the adventure. And that’s where my entire remote work journey started.

After that, I moved to Mexico City for 5 months. And then, I lived in Playa del Carmen for some time, too.

In 2018, I took it a step further: instead of living in one city at a time, I started moving constantly… like literally all the time.

For about eight months, I moved to a new city almost every month, living out of one suitcase and a carry-on with everything I owned inside those. I started in Monterrey, then Boquete (small town Panama), then Buenos Aires again, Santiago, Lima, Cali and back to Monterrey.

It was fun.

It was also… a lot.

The perks (because yes, it’s amazing)

There are real reasons people fall in love with the digital nomad life:

Freedom & flexibility. You can work from different places and build your days around what you want. You sort of get a local experience because you’re not just there for a week.

Living in different places. New cultures, new food, new routines, new experiences. For someone who loves traveling, this is the ultimate dream.

Meeting people. You can connect with locals, or with other digital nomads who are doing the same thing because you’re not just there on vacation.

Lower cost of living. You can intentionally choose cities where your money stretches further — which can free up cash for travel or other goals. For the most part, I tried to do this.

So yes: it’s an incredible lifestyle if you can manage it.

But, what made me stop?

And, what’s the right way to do this without burning out?
